name: Bianca Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Halvorsen's, a family garage in a small town, the kind with a calendar from the parts supplier on the wall and a radio that only gets one station. Erik Halvorsen took me on as an apprentice when I was twenty-two, and I'm still learning, slower than I'd like. I do services, clutches with Erik watching, exhausts, and a lot of farm trucks and old hatchbacks. I like that I know most customers by their car before I know their name.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's home like, and how do you feel about new technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Luka, he drives a delivery van for a parcel firm. We rent a small house near the station, and we've got about three months saved. I don't use AI, I don't trust it and I don't need it, I've got Erik's notebooks. I'm not against it for other people, it's just not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, nothing to see then, back to work. I'm not one for big opinions online, I'd probably just shrug. At the garage I'd tell Erik his notebooks beat any chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it doesn't change much, but that doesn't mean I'm relaxed. Erik's sixty-six and talks about retiring, and his son lives in the city and doesn't want the garage. The thing that scares me isn't a computer, it's the day my boss hands back the keys to the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, try to get better at diagnostics with Erik before he goes. Keep putting about a hundred a month away. Maybe ask Erik straight out what his plan is, which I've been avoiding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like when a car makes a noise you can't place. Not panic, just a niggle that won't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Erik retired next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look at the two other garages in town, or the dealership twenty minutes away. I'd rather stay local, I like knowing the customers. I'm not sure I'm good enough yet to walk into a new place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you thought about taking over the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luka's asked me that. I don't have the money or the skills yet, and running a business scares me. Maybe in ten years.

say: I'd **shrug it off** and get back to work, without posting opinions.
I'd tell Erik his **notebooks beat** any chatbot.
think: My real worry is Erik **retiring** with no one taking over the garage.
AI changing nothing doesn't make my **job secure**.
do: Learn **diagnostics** from Erik before he retires.
Keep saving **a hundred a month** and ask Erik about his plans.
feel: Feels **uneasy**, like an unplaced noise in a car that won't go away.
S0.quote: The thing that scares me isn't a computer, it's the day my boss hands back the keys to the garage.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **owner retiring**, not technology.
She lacks **confidence** to walk into a new garage.
Taking over the business feels too **risky** to her for now.

steps.text: Learn diagnostics from Erik before he retires
Ask Erik directly about his retirement plans
Keep saving a hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to sort the people who adapt from the people who don't, and I'm honestly not sure which I am. I wouldn't post about it. At work I'd just keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's worse for me than I'd admit. If the new scan tools tell you everything, Erik could sell to someone who buys one and hires a cheaper kid instead of me. And the parcel firm already plans Luka's routes by computer. I'm the person in the garage who refuses to touch a computer, and that person is the one who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Erik to teach me his diagnostics properly and maybe let me try the scan box. I'd push savings to two hundred, cut the second car we're thinking of buying. If I had to, I'd try one of the AI tools, but I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm stubborn, and stubborn doesn't always win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Luka's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Routes are already planned by a computer, so that part's done. It's the driving that pays, and robots are slow to arrive here. But if the firm saves money, it might cut drivers anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd try AI only if you had to. When would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day a customer tells me the chatbot already said what's wrong with their car. That's probably not far off.

say: I'd say the change **sorts people** into those who adapt and those who don't.
I'd keep **my head down** at work and post nothing.
think: As the one who **avoids computers**, I'd likely be the first to go.
A buyer could replace me with **a scan tool** and a cheaper junior.
do: Ask Erik to teach **proper diagnostics** with the scan box.
Raise savings to **two hundred** and drop plans for a second car.
feel: Feels **anxious**, because her **stubbornness** might not win this time.
S1.quote: I'm the person in the garage who refuses to touch a computer, and that person is the one who goes.
fieldNote: She admits her **resistance** puts her at risk.
Luka's **driving job** adds a second household worry.
Her trigger to try AI is a **customer** knowing more than her.

steps.text: Ask Erik to teach her the scan box
Drop plans to buy a second car
Raise savings to two hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, nobody's ready, and I'd mean it. I'd probably just say that to Erik and Luka, not online. I'd tell my mum to stop worrying, while worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, 2028 is the end of me needing to think on the job, and 2031 is the end of the hands. Luka's van drives itself by then too, probably. In five years both of us could be out of work, and I've got three months of rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I'd keep working, save everything, and maybe ask my parents if we could move in with them if it came to it. I wouldn't know what to retrain into, because everything I can think of is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Overwhelmed. It's like someone opened the bonnet and every part is broken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd start doing now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saving harder, that's all I can think of. And maybe talking to Luka about what we'd give up. I don't have a plan, and that's the worst part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your parents help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would, they've got a house with a spare room. It'd feel like going backwards, but I'd do it.

say: I'd call it **madness** that nobody is ready for.
I'd say it only to **Erik and Luka**, not online.
think: By 2031 both my **hands-on job** and Luka's driving could be gone.
With **three months** of rent saved, we'd have little room.
do: Save **everything possible** while still working at the garage.
Ask her **parents** about moving in if it came to it.
feel: Feels **overwhelmed**, like every part under the bonnet is broken.
S2.quote: In five years both of us could be out of work, and I've got three months of rent in the bank.
fieldNote: She has **no retraining idea**, because everything she knows seems at risk.
Her **parents' spare room** is her safety net.
She expects **both incomes** to go within five years.

steps.text: Save every spare amount from both wages
Ask her parents about moving into their spare room
Keep working at Halvorsen's as long as it lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives people some time, but it's still fast. I'd mostly keep it to myself. Erik would say he'll be retired by then, lucky him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's not much better than two years for someone like me. I'm slow to change, so five years just means five years of dread. Some people would use five years to plan, but I'd probably spend those five years worrying instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, at least. Maybe ask about the electric course at the college, since Erik always says that's the future. I'd keep saving, and Luka and I would talk about the cheapest place we could live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. Only slightly less than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help you use the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone telling me exactly what to train in, with proof it'll still be there. I'm not going to gamble on something new without proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only nearer my parents, not to a city. I'd rather be poor near family than rich among strangers.

say: I'd say **five years** gives people some time, but it's still fast.
I'd mostly **keep it to myself** and let Erik joke about being retired.
think: For someone **slow to change**, five years is just five years of dread.
I'd likely spend the time **worrying rather than planning**.
do: Ask the college about the **electric course**.
Talk with Luka about the **cheapest place** to live, near her parents.
feel: Feels **alarmed**, only a little less than in the fast picture.
S3.quote: Some people would use five years to plan, but I'd probably spend those five years worrying instead.
fieldNote: She wants **proof** before training in anything new.
She'd stay near **family** rather than chase jobs elsewhere.
The extra time barely helps her **mood**, though she'd try.

steps.text: Ask the college about its electric vehicle course
Look with Luka for cheaper housing near her parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough for most people to sort themselves out. I'd probably say it to Luka over dinner. At work it'd become a joke for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough to learn something properly, even for me. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI arrives and forty for robots. Ten years is long enough for even a slow learner like me to get good at something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electric course over a couple of years and learn the scan tools. I'd save steadily and maybe consider starting a family once things felt clearer. If Erik retired, I'd go to the dealership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could manage it. There's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at forty if the robots arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope by then to be the person who checks the robots' work. Or something else entirely, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably wait a few years. Kids feel like something you plan for when things are stable.

say: I'd say **a decade** is enough for most people.
It would become **a joke** at work for a while.
think: Even a **slow learner** like me could master something new in ten years.
do: Take the **electric course** over two years and learn scan tools.
Move to the **dealership** if Erik retires.
Wait a few years before **starting a family**.
feel: Feels **anxious** but manageable, with **room to breathe**.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for even a slow learner like me to get good at something new.
fieldNote: The decade gives her **confidence** that she can learn.
She'd **delay children** until things feel stable.
She still has **no clear picture** of her role after robots.

steps.text: Take the electric course over two years
Apply to the dealership if Erik retires
Wait a few years before trying for children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no plan and neither would Luka. What would help is someone telling me exactly what to train in, with proof, and help with rent while we figure it out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small towns. In a small town there are only so many jobs, and when the garage closes, people don't just get another one around the corner.

headlineQuote: In a small town there are only so many jobs, and when the garage closes, people don't just get another one around the corner.
portrait: Bianca is an **apprentice-trained** junior at a small-town family garage.
She **never uses AI**, trusting her boss's notebooks instead.
She rents with Luka, a **delivery driver**, and they have about three months saved.
Her first worry is her **boss retiring**, and fast AGI leaves her without a plan.
With more time, she believes even a **slow learner** can retrain.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Luka could both lose work with no plan.
whatWouldHelp: Clear, **proven advice** on what to train in, plus **rent support** during the change.
